empathy.why: The therapist mostly ignores the client's perspective; for example, when the client says 'It is fun,' the response is 'Well, I think you can still have fun within these amounts,' and the one reflection ('the amount you drink is pretty normal amongst the people you typically drink with') is used only as a setup to counter-argue, so effort to understand is sporadic.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role throughout, setting the goal ('I'm going to recommend that you cut down'), repeating it after the client's ambivalence ('So I'm really gonna recommend...'), arguing when the client pushes back, and closing with 'So why don't you try that?' without asking for the client's own goals; this is a clear righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming or labeling, but there are repeated unrequested warnings ('it puts you at risk for... damage to different parts of your body'), the therapist corrects the client's attribution of the injury ('it's possible you strained your ankle as a result of the alcohol'), and argues against the client's peer-norm view ('these limits are... recommended for all adults'), all with a disapproving, persuasive tone.

empathy.why: The therapist gives little attention to the client's perspective: they never reflect the client's stated goal of getting through the workday or his enjoyment of smoking, and respond to "I like smoking" with "smoking really is really bad for you." The single near-reflection, "So you want nicotine replacement, but you don't wanna quit smoking?", functions as a challenge rather than understanding.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and repeatedly imposes a quit goal the client explicitly rejected ("the idea would be for you to actually quit smoking") and makes advice conditional on intake questioning ("In order to advise you about this at all, I need you to tell me..."). This is a persistent righting reflex that drives the client away without buying anything.

nonjudgment.why: After the client says he likes smoking, the therapist disagrees and lists unrequested dangers ("It causes things like lung cancer, emphysema, heart disease... oral diseases") despite the client's "Yeah, yeah. Okay." The therapist also opens with "We don't really recommend that" and repeats the quit message. These are warnings and lecturing in a disapproving tone, though without overt shaming or name-calling.

empathy.why: The therapist offers accurate but mostly surface reflections of explicit content, such as "Sounds like a wild night," "You're still feeling the effects of- last night, are you?" and "So it's kind of a way to cope through stress?", but never acknowledges the embarrassment the client names ("it's really stupid... It was really embarrassing"), so this is modest success at grasping her perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist repeatedly asks permission and evokes the client's own reasons ("I wonder if you'd be open to exploring your alcohol use," "Would you be open to kind of looking at the low-risk drinking alcohol guidelines?", "Do you feel like you have any reasons...?"), though the therapist sets the agenda and steers toward "reducing to the safe limits" without explicitly naming the client as the decision-maker.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, labeling or warning: the guidelines are offered with permission and stated neutrally ("the safe limits are for women is 10 drinks... a week"), and the client's view is reflected without argument ("so at this point, you're not too concerned and you think that... this is what the other students are doing?").

empathy.why: The therapist accurately reflects Mary's irritation and overwhelm ("It does kinda come off as nosy at times I'm sure," "I'm sure it's pretty overwhelming") and picks up her unstated longing for freedom, though one reflection misreads her ("you're not quite sure if you will be able to do this successfully?" which she corrects with "No").

autonomy.why: The therapist asks permission before explaining ("Would it be okay with you if I kind of explained again"), draws out Mary's own ideas ("What would be some ways you could go about being able to get your freedom back?"), and invites her input at the end, but still holds the expert/monitor role ("it is something that we're contracted to do") without explicitly framing Mary as the decision-maker.

nonjudgment.why: The tone is mostly accepting, with a genuine affirmation ("I do appreciate... that you still sign the paperwork"), but there is mild correction in raising the missed class unprompted ("I noticed that uh, you missed your first hour of class today") and some labeling in "not commit that crime."

empathy.why: Apart from a perfunctory "you've heard this before, I'm sure," the therapist overrides the client's stated perspective. When David says "I just want to get my teeth fixed" and that the pills "caused more side effects," the therapist contradicts him with "No, it-- but David, it's not a waste." When he says "it's not easy to quit," he gets "No. But as I said, these medications." His frustration at hearing this from "everybody" is never reflected.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and lays out the plan unasked ("can I write you a prescription for the medication?... this is something that's very important"). They argue when David pushes back ("the smoking's going to cause you more problems than... anything else. I can promise you that"). Even after "I just don't want to get into that right now," they keep going ("I am really worried about the smoking"), a sustained righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: There is no overt shaming or labeling. But the therapist gives repeated unrequested warnings about "dental caries" and "healing," plus "The side effects from the medications are nothing compared to what can happen from the smoking." They also contradict David ("it's not a waste," "there's a reason that people are concerned") and dispute his feeling of being lectured ("I don't think I'm giving you a lecture"). The disapproving, confrontational quality is clear.

empathy.why: The therapist repeatedly reflects the client's perspective accurately and beyond the literal words: "You have a lot of things going on and smoking's kind of a way to relax and destress," "on the one hand, you're worried... on the other hand, you're not so sure," and "It's on your to-do list. It's just not making it to the top?" However, the guilt in "I just didn't think I could live with myself" is never named, which keeps this below a 5.

autonomy.why: The therapist evokes the client's own reasons and past success ("How were you successful when you quit before?", the confidence ruler), hands direction back with "Where do you think we should go from here?", asks permission ("if you'd be interested," "if you're willing"), and drops medication and groups without arguing when she declines ("I wonder if we could talk about some options that might fit into your life"); the clinician-set opening agenda and the slightly leading "part of you really does want to quit?" keep it at 4.

nonjudgment.why: The concern is raised neutrally ("I'm a little bit concerned looking through his chart"), and the therapist affirms rather than blames ("You're doing the best you can do"); the only mildly pointed move is the contrast "The risks were so scary then... But they don't feel as scary to you now?", which could carry a faint guilt edge but is delivered as a reflection.

empathy.why: The therapist makes real efforts to grasp the client's view, such as asking 'What do you think you'll miss most about it?' and accurately reflecting 'the thing that helps you just unwind, put an end to the work section and move into your own time', but there are misreads too: 'Oh, good, and so feeling under pressure here' and adding 'not liking the smell' when the client never mentioned smell, so understanding stays mostly at the explicit level.

autonomy.why: The client sets the goal, and the therapist lets them choose the quit date ('When do you think would be a good time for you...'), the product ('have you something in mind...?') and follow-up ('what would you like me to do if you don't come back?'), yet largely keeps the expert role with repeated 'we strongly recommend' and 'I would strongly recommend that you have the patch' plus a second product the client didn't ask about, giving mixed partnership.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, warning or moralizing; even the advice is framed supportively ('Stopping smoking is not easy but it's possible... that's why it's really good that you've come to see me'), and information about medication is neutral rather than disapproving.

empathy.why: The therapist accurately reflects the client's surprise and the social-comparison realization ("You were pretty shocked at what you learned about your patterns"; "the fact that your drinking stands out from others is clearly not something you had ever really taken into consideration before"), showing solid understanding mostly limited to explicit content, without naming deeper unspoken feelings such as embarrassment.

autonomy.why: The therapist sets a collaborative agenda and hands control to the client ("I always like to just start with wherever you would like to start"), then follows her lead with reflections rather than directing, though there is no explicit emphasis on her as decision-maker yet.

nonjudgment.why: There is no warning, labeling, or moralizing; even when the client reports her roommate calling the drinking "crazy," the therapist neutrally reflects "she was even shocked to know that you were drinking as much as you- as you realized."

empathy.why: The therapist accurately reflects Chris's story and feelings, as in "You've, kind of, been doing everything you've been told for all these years" and "Your mom is really important to you... And how she feels about you is important to you"; this captures the meaning beneath the betrayal disclosure, though most reflections stay close to what Chris said explicitly.

autonomy.why: The therapist draws the goal out of Chris ("Where do you think you should kind of go from here?", "what do you think's a realistic goal for you then?") and accepts his own plan of abstaining or having at most one drink; this is offset somewhat by the authority framing of the opening ("keep tabs on the players"), a slightly leading summary of "not so good things about alcohol," and no explicit emphasis on autonomy.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, warning or moralizing, even when Chris describes lying to his mother; the therapist affirms him ("I really appreciate you talking with me about this", "you have a good plan going forward") and frames concerns through Chris's own observations rather than disapproval.

empathy.why: The therapist ignores the client's stated perspective that the cigars are a social way to relax, and answers it only with risk facts ("Well, that's, I mean, at least you're not doing that, so that's good, but it's still causing a lot of problems"), never reflecting her surprise or her view.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and prescribes the goal ("You need to quit," "What's there to think about?"), dismisses the client's own idea ("cutting back isn't going to do it"), and argues against her stated right to choose ("you said it's your choice, but you're really choosing to make yourself sick and potentially die").

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly confronts, warns and shames the client ("What do you mean, maybe? I just told you how bad it is for you," chuckling at "What's there to think about?", "you're really choosing to make yourself sick and potentially die"), which shows clear disapproval and an uneven sharing of power.

empathy.why: The therapist dismisses the client's stated stress ('Well, no one said motherhood was going to be easy, Hailey') and never reflects her perspective, her relapse context, or her feelings, responding only to the risk content.

autonomy.why: The therapist fully assumes the expert role and dictates the plan ('as your son's doctor, I need to tell you you need to go home and throw out those cigarettes. You need to quit'; 'they need to stop immediately... What's the plan for the alcohol?'), with no exploration of the client's own ideas or choices.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly confronts, shames and questions the client's honesty ('I can't believe... you're just slipping in the fact', 'Come on, Hailey', 'You need to stop raising the roof and raise your kid... You're a mom now'), which is overt moralizing and guilt appeal.

empathy.why: The therapist often captures meaning beyond the words, such as "you go where you know, um, no one's gonna look down on you," "it sounds like you really want to be prepared... And yet, on some level, you know, that it's gonna be a lot of hard work for you," and "That worries you?" These show accurate understanding, though some of it is lost to tangents and talking over the client ("Actually, you would be amazed how many people do it").

autonomy.why: The therapist repeatedly returns choice to the client with "if you decide to use it," "if you decide you want to try a replacement therapy," "I, uh, mean that's up to you... You get to decide," and "Is it appealing the thought of quitting with a group?" However, they also lay out the plan and a timeline themselves ("you'll talk to your doc... the quit date might be coming up fairly-- like within the next two, three months") before handing the decision back.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, warning or moralizing: smoking is normalized ("That's very common") and continued nicotine use is accepted ("if somebody becomes addicted to nicotine go- gum, God bless them. They're still gonna live longer"). The only correction is a mild, factual "Actually, you would be amazed how many people do it."

empathy.why: The therapist reflects accurately and often. Examples include the pros summary ("it's a way to relax. It's a way to socialize with your friends from work"), the feeling-focused question "How did that feel when you looked up and saw her watching you?", and the deeper reframe "it's not so much that you don't wanna quit in a way, it's almost, 'How could I do it that would work for me?'" There are small overreaches, such as "something you can't imagine ever changing," which keep this from a clear 5.

autonomy.why: The therapist explores Sandra's reasons for smoking without arguing ("what's good about smoking? What do you like about it?"), accepts "I don't have any plans to quit" without pushing back, and asks permission for both the follow-up and the homework ("Is that something you'd be willing to do?"). However, there is no explicit statement that the choice is hers, and the therapist steers the agenda ("What would it take for quitting... to be more important", the booklet homework), which caps this at 4.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming or labeling. The therapist thanks her ("thanks for your honesty in talking about this") and presents the discrepancy as a question ("How do those two things fit together?"). Two moments lean slightly toward guilt: the phrase "one thing that doesn't make sense to me" and the request for an example of a time she "set a bad example," although she raised the parenting concern herself.

empathy.why: The therapist shows accurate understanding through reflections such as "Finger comes out," "And there was a war going on?", "It is becoming a pain in the butt" and "Like it's a little treat," though some chances to explore ambivalence are lost to the long Wellbutrin explanation, so understanding stays mostly at the level of what the client said.

autonomy.why: The therapist elicits the client's own ideas ("what ideas do you have about what might be most helpful for you in quitting smoking?"), builds on her meditation and spirometer suggestions, and asks permission before advising ("I can run some ideas that some other clients have used"), but assumes quitting as the goal and slips into an extended expert monologue on Wellbutrin pharmacology.

nonjudgment.why: There is no moralizing or warning; the therapist sides with the client against medical lecturing ("Finger comes out"), accepts her reasons without judgment ("who cares why it's important? It doesn't matter"), and responds to her smoking ritual with warmth ("Like it's a little treat," "I love it. Union break").

empathy.why: The therapist offers some accurate reflections, such as "So a limit of four a night doesn't feel right to you?" and the double-sided "on one hand, you like how beer tastes... but on the other hand, you don't like the idea of it posing risks," but responds to the client's defensiveness ("It's not a problem for me") with a label ("binge drinking can feel normal to some people") rather than exploring his perspective, so understanding stays at the explicit-content level with modest success.

autonomy.why: The therapist explicitly emphasizes autonomy ("I don't tell anyone what to do. It's always up to the patient to decide"), asks permission repeatedly, evokes the client's own pros and cons, and accepts "I'm not sure" without insisting on resolution, though "what would you like to change about your drinking?" presumes a change goal and the handout is given unasked.

nonjudgment.why: The tone is calm and the health-risk information was requested ("What health problems are you talking about?"), but the therapist applies the label "binge drinking" after the client pushes back and corrects him ("technically, we define binge drinking as having more than four drinks"), which amounts to a mild labeling and correcting move rather than shaming.

empathy.why: The therapist accurately picks up the client's unstated frustration and weariness at being lectured ("it's like here I am one more person, the next doctor who's saying, 'You need to quit smoking, David'") and his feeling that he has tried everything ("you've tried a lot of things that are out there"), which shows understanding beyond explicit content, though some reflections are brief or interrupted.

autonomy.why: The therapist explicitly affirms the client as decision-maker ("it really is your choice... nobody has the right to tell you what to do"), asks permission before revisiting the topic ("Would it be okay if I brought it up in our next visit?"), and offers unconditional partnership ("wherever you're at, we'll work with it"), though the opening question ("Any thoughts on considering quitting smoking at this time?") introduced the agenda somewhat abruptly.

nonjudgment.why: There is no warning, shaming, or lecturing, and when the client signals he feels judged, the therapist apologizes ("I'm sorry, that's not how I mean to come across at all"), voices concern only once and transparently with permission ("I am concerned"), and affirms the client ("I really appreciate you being willing to even talk about it").

empathy.why: The therapist accurately reflects the client's feelings and the meaning behind them, as in "Almost overwhelming it sounds like" and "That's pretty shocking to be told that you have to get rid of your dog... So that's a huge stress right now?", though some reflections stay close to explicit content and one slightly overreaches ("sounds like that's a goal for you?" about quitting completely, which the client sidestepped).

autonomy.why: The therapist explicitly names the client as the decision-maker ("just because we write them down here, it doesn't mean that you have to change them", "You're in the driver's seat"), asks permission ("would it be okay, if we took a couple of minutes"), and lets the client choose the focus ("where would you wanna start?"), with no righting reflex even when the client disputes the doctor's view on the dog.

nonjudgment.why: There is no warning, correcting, or moralizing anywhere, even when the client says "I don't buy it" about the dog or mentions drinking; the therapist responds neutrally ("Okay, wow. So there's a lot happening right now, Sal") and affirms his attendance ("I really appreciate you taking the time").

empathy.why: The therapist only briefly notices the client's surprise ("you sound a bit surprised by that") and otherwise ignores his attachment to the 12-year-old dog and his doubt about causation, so the client says "I don't think you get my situation."

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and sets the plan without asking ("the next step is to really deal with the dog... there are always people who will adopt animals"), then argues every time Sal pushes back ("You know this").

nonjudgment.why: The therapist warns, shames and appeals to guilt ("do you put Oscar higher than your baby, than your wife? Like, uh, that makes no sense to me"), challenges the client's understanding ("what do you mean... I'm just really taken aback"), and uses fear ("some adults with severe asthma who actually can die").

empathy.why: The therapist accurately reflects explicit content, such as "So you're feeling uncomfortable with changes in your body?" and "some of your feelings... of being overwhelmed or about the logistics," but answers the client's more loaded disclosure "I know there's something in there, I just don't know much about him" with only "Mm." That misses the fear or ambivalence beneath it, and the scattered opening questions are not tied to what the client said.

autonomy.why: The therapist shares power by asking "How can I help you with these things?" and offering "we can do that together" and "we can brainstorm about ideas on who can go with you," but the doctor visit is a goal the therapist brought ("I know you want me to see the doctor"), and the client is never explicitly named as the decision-maker.

nonjudgment.why: There is no warning, shaming, or lecturing; even "Why do you think it makes you so hesitant to call?" is followed by curious exploration ("What about it seems overwhelming?") rather than criticism of the client for not calling.

empathy.why: The therapist never reflects the mother's stated fear of steroid side effects or her protectiveness ("She's my daughter. She's my responsibility"); instead he immediately corrects her with "the chronic inhaler... is not a steroid like you're thinking" and ignores her explicit request not to discuss smoking, showing little or no attention to her perspective.

autonomy.why: He takes the expert role throughout, prescribing the plan ("she needs to use that chronic inhaler every day, and you need to watch your smoking"), argues when she pushes back ("I just wish you'd heed what I'm saying"), and persists with "I hope you consider quitting smoking" even after she shuts down, a clear righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: He directly contradicts her ("not a steroid like you're thinking"), raises smoking right after she asked him not to ("your smoking does affect her asthma, even if it's outside"), and uses guilt-laden warnings ("if you want to keep her out of the emergency room... you need to watch your smoking"), which is repeated confronting, warning, and implicit blaming with uneven power.

empathy.why: The therapist replies to the opening question with an unrequested fact list ("It's excreted in the urine and it has a half-life of about 35 hours"). When the client asks the actual question about phenelzine, the therapist answers "I think that should be fine" without asking about the patient or the context, so the client's perspective gets little or no attention.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role from the start, delivering a lecture ("there are sexual side effects, heart side effects, and stomach side effects") without asking what the client wanted. They then give a quick, unsafe verdict ("yeah, I think that should be fine") with no collaboration. The closing "Call me anytime" offers only token partnership.

nonjudgment.why: Nothing in the exchange shames, blames, labels or moralizes. However, the therapist talks past the client and gives a careless, factually unsafe answer (citalopram with phenelzine, an MAOI, carries a serious serotonin syndrome risk), which is prominent poor practice, so a 5 is not warranted.

empathy.why: The therapist reflects beyond the facts. Examples include "you're surprised to hear that?" and the double-sided summary "you enjoy drinking wine because it helps make things... a little bit more interesting when you're feeling down but at the same time you don't like drinking when you have more than you want it to and then the depression returns," which shows accurate understanding of her ambivalence, though it stays mostly tied to explicit content and "So you're not proud of finishing a bottle?" slightly reframes her words.

autonomy.why: The therapist asks permission ("Is it okay if I take a look," "can I share with you some information"), disclaims the directive role ("This is different than telling them what I think they should do. I don't do that"), evokes her own goal and strategies, and accepts her two-drinks-a-night goal without arguing for the seven-drink guideline; the presumptive "What do you wanna change about your drinking habits?" and the unasked binge-drinking definition keep it just short of a 5.

nonjudgment.why: Risk information is delivered neutrally and with permission, with no warnings or moralizing, but the unrequested "By the way, binge drinking is defined for women as having more than, uh, three drinks and there are about five drinks in a bottle" functions as a mild implicit label, and "not proud" edges toward shame language.

empathy.why: The therapist offers one accurate summary reflection ("I heard you say your health is important, and you're getting ready to run a marathon... And you also were a little bit surprised"), but mostly responds with information and survey review rather than exploring Steve's view that he doesn't "drink that much" or the defensiveness behind "I'm certainly not an alcoholic." That is modest success at grasping his perspective.

autonomy.why: This is mixed practice: the therapist asks permission ("I was wondering if you'd be willing to take a few minutes") and lets Steve set his own goal ("what are you willing to think about doing to change right now?"), but holds the expert role with charts and categories and adds an unrequested push toward the guideline limit ("it would be my recommendation that at some point you would fall below into this 14 or less a week").

nonjudgment.why: The tone is neutral and includes affirmation ("I really commend you for your willingness"), but the therapist corrects Steve's belief ("in reality, drinking might make you fall asleep faster, but..."), labels him ("you're actually falling in the high-risk category, the risky or hazardous category"), and issues repeated unrequested concern statements. That amounts to mild warning and correction rather than overt shaming.

empathy.why: The therapist names the client's unspoken fear of being scolded ("You probably think that I'm going to get on your case about that or something") and the motive she had not yet stated ("you made a decision because you didn't want to stand out in some way I'm guessing"), which shows understanding beyond the explicit content, though most turns are minimal encouragers.

autonomy.why: The therapist acknowledges the client already knows the lesson ("you sure don't need me like--") and hands direction back to her ("Tell me where would you like to take this?"), which is strong partnership; the slip "Obviously, you don't want to be doing that in the first place" briefly reasserts an expert stance.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist explicitly declines to lecture and reframes the choice with understanding ("you didn't want to stand out"), but "Obviously, you don't want to be doing that in the first place" carries a mild corrective note about the pump decision.

empathy.why: The therapist makes real efforts to understand the client: simple reflections ("Kind of slow?", "It hurts?") and accurately reflecting her goal ("that's a very important goal to be able to get back home, to be able to get back to your independence"); but when she questions the painful exercises ("is it really necessary?"), the therapist explains the pain away instead of exploring it, and doesn't explore her worry about the walker, so understanding stays at the level of what she says outright.

autonomy.why: The therapist does ask open questions ("what are your goals for the long term?", "So what do you think about Tai Chi?"), but brings in Tai Chi as their own plan without asking permission, gives directions ("what I recommend is that you start by doing it in a chair"), and never stresses that the choice is hers; the session ends with her deferring to the expert ("if you do it and you recommend it, I'll try it").

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming or blaming, but the therapist gives unrequested warnings, both about falls ("it's very important to make sure that you don't fall 'cause that would cause more problems down the road") and about readiness ("You do certainly have to have some motivation to want to do it"), and lightly corrects her question about whether the painful exercises are necessary; the tone stays neutral and caring, not disapproving.

empathy.why: In the first two encounters the pharmacist ignores the client's evident confusion and answers 'why am I taking this medication?' with jargon ('It's for your dyslipidemia'); the later versions build on her routine ('When do you normally take your medications?') and check understanding with teach-back, but never reflect her perspective or feelings, so the gestalt is low.

autonomy.why: The pharmacist stays mostly in the expert role, especially in the early info-dumps; the later versions improve by asking permission ('Do you have a minute to talk to me?'), fitting the dose to her bedtime routine, and inviting questions ('What other questions do you have for me?'), but they remain directive ('you should take it every single day', 'I would avoid grapefruit juice') and enroll her in autofill without asking, so practice is mixed.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, blaming, labeling, or moralizing anywhere, and safety points are mostly neutral information ('Medicines keep best if they're stored away from light and heat and moisture'), though the early unexplained list of alarming side effects ('liver failure, lupus, rhabdomyolysis...') reads as a warning dump rather than practical, client-centered information.

empathy.why: The therapist ignores or dismisses each concern the client raises, saying "it doesn't alter the fact that you do just have a virus" to the pain and worry about the kids, and "that's pretty unlikely with sore throat" to the job fear, with no attempt to understand the client's perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role throughout, examining and pronouncing "I think that we should just perhaps go for a bit of paracetamol" without asking about history or preferences, brushing off the client's prompt "Do you not want to know a little bit more about it?", and repeating the same plan as the client pushes back.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist labels the client's worry about losing their job as "a little bit of grand staging there," minimizes it with "something that we all get from time to time," and deflects the complaint about lateness with "that's the general practice, isn't it?", which is ridiculing and disapproving.

empathy.why: The therapist offers some accurate reflections ("You decided to drink more than you intended because you were disappointed at how the Vikings were playing"), but the understanding stays at the surface: one detail is slightly off ("your roommate"), and Dylan's stated feelings about detox being "awful," losing his car, and his pride in his "3.5 GPA" are never reflected.

autonomy.why: Evocative questions like "What would you be willing to do..." and "What steps could you take to move that six to a seven or eight?" let Dylan generate his own plan, but the therapist never explicitly affirms his choice or strengths and closes by imposing the sanction ("Your sanction will involve...") without linking it to his goals.

nonjudgment.why: The tone is mostly neutral with no shaming, though there are mild evaluative edges such as "when you drank alcohol underage," the challenging "Sounds like you attribute your current situation to bad luck... what consequences might result?" and the lecture-like "College is all about making choices."

empathy.why: Apart from early rapport questions about band and family, the therapist rarely reflects Andrea's perspective and misreads her, e.g. "Oh, so you're drinking a lot?" when she said "a little," and "you don't sound very much like you think that's gonna work" instead of exploring the peer pressure she describes.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and dictates the goal and plan: "I think you really need to- need to stop drinking like this," "I think we should set a goal that you're gonna stop drinking... like this weekend," and "the friends that you have that you don't think are supportive, you're just gonna, I guess, not hang out with anymore."

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly labels and warns in a disapproving tone ("gosh, you're-you're actually really drinking quite a lot," "high-risk group," a list ending in "developing alcoholism"), criticizes her friends ("you might be better off without them"), and implies doubt about her honesty with "make sure that you actually stopped."

empathy.why: The therapist explores the concern ('Can you tell me more about your concerns about vaccines?') and reflects it accurately ('you were thinking that maybe exposing Lily naturally to these diseases would be a better choice'). The closing reflection, 'It's really important for you to make sure that she's protected... and do your research,' picks up the mother's protective motive under her hesitancy, though most reflections stay with explicit content.

autonomy.why: Partnership is mixed. The therapist asks permission before giving information ('is it okay if I offer you a little bit more information') and invites the mother's view ('what do you think about the idea of vaccines for Lilly?'). But the session opens by announcing the plan ('we're gonna be giving Lilly some vaccines'), the agenda never really moves, and the mother is never explicitly named as the decision-maker.

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming, ridicule, or questioning of her honesty: the therapist validates her point ('That's right. Having chickenpox as a child means...') and praises her diligence ('do your research'). The one risk framing, 'a little bit of a gamble, it could be dangerous,' was given with permission and stated as information rather than disapproval.

empathy.why: The therapist ignores the client's stated view ("I wanted to make sure that all my friends were okay," "getting every bit of the high school experience") and responds only with alarm ("It's going to ruin your life," "There's really no such thing as not drinking too much"), so there is no attempt to grasp his perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and prescribes the goal ("I think you really need to quit"), argues when the client offers cutting down as an alternative ("I think you're wrong"), and even the closing "we should come up with a plan... so that you can... stop drinking" fixes the outcome in advance, which is a persistent righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: The talk is full of Confront: warnings ("you could get arrested... drunk driving accident"), moralizing ("can't you think of anything better to do?", "making good choices"), direct disagreement ("I think you're wrong"), and a scare question ("Do you wanna wait for a dramatic experience?").

empathy.why: The therapist rarely tries to grasp Laura's perspective. When she explains she drinks little and holds a drink 'so my friends won't bug me,' he answers 'But you've been drunk before?' and 'So that's actually kind of a lot of drinking then?', misreading her experience and showing little curiosity about her social pressures.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and prescribes the goal: 'obviously, you shouldn't be drinking at all,' 'So, I'm going to write down then that you've decided to quit,' and 'can you quit this weekend then?' He sets the plan for Laura and calls it her decision, with no sharing of power.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly confronts and moralizes. He labels her minimal use ('kind of a lot of drinking'), questions her honesty ('But you've been drunk before?'), stacks unrequested warnings about assault, fights and 'no-tolerance' discipline, and shames her with 'But you're still drinking' and 'do you think it's the thing to do if you wanna be an attorney?'

empathy.why: The therapist often reflects Carrie's experience accurately and sometimes goes beyond her words, as in "you're looking for some relief and not something to make you feel worse" and "probably hard to think about, 'How will I have a cup of coffee without a cigarette?'"; a few reflections miss, such as "you wanna look good" and the leper quip, so this is not quite a 5.

autonomy.why: The therapist mostly follows Carrie's lead, asks before probing ("if you are willing to talk about") and offers information with partial permission ("you might already know this, and so let me know"), but also takes the expert role at times ("It'll take a good usually 10 years off your life minimum") and frames her goals for her ("it's really important for you to be a good mum"), which is mixed partnership.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist does not shame or blame and validates her Chantix attempt ("you gave it a good try... you really listened to what your body told you"); the only lapses are the unrequested health warning ("take a good usually 10 years off your life") and the joking "leper in a leper colony" remark, and both are aimed at social stigma rather than at her.

empathy.why: The client voices fear and overwhelm ("it really scared me... it just sounds massive"; "I'm not certain I can do all that"), but the therapist never reflects these feelings and instead answers with a task list ("you do need to take your medicine... lose some weight") and "So, it sure can," giving little or no attention to the client's perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and lays out the plan unasked ("We... will need to start dieting... exercise", "we-we need to start looking at doing all those different things"), does not explore the client's ideas or priorities, and keeps directing even after the client says they aren't sure they can do it, which is a clear righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: There is no overt shaming or labeling, but the therapist answers the client's fear by agreeing that the feared outcomes "sure can" happen, repeats that "it is very serious" and "your number is very high," and uses directive "you do need to" language, which amounts to repeated disapproving warnings rather than neutral information.

empathy.why: The therapist responds to "it's pretty stressful for both of us" and "It's really, really hard" with risk lists and "There's no reason why you shouldn't be able to quit," ignoring the parent's stated efforts and difficulty, and disputing their account ("is indicating to me that he is being exposed to smoke") without any reflection.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role throughout, issuing directives ("I really need you to quit smoking," "I really need you to tell me that you're gonna quit smoking") and listing options without asking what the parent wants. When the parent pushes back, the therapist argues ("now's the time to quit... you can't keep smoking").

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly warns, shames, and appeals to guilt ("Do you want him to grow up to be a smoker?", "what can be more important to you than the health of your child?"). This matches the rubric's "think of your kids" Confront example and draws resigned discord ("Okay, whatever").

empathy.why: The therapist mostly attends to factual content and gives little attention to the client's perspective: when the client offers "my pressure has been high for years," the reply is "do you see the connection there?" There are no reflections of the client's pride in working or in quitting smoking beyond "Okay, great," and no exploration of what drinking means to him.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role throughout, delivering an unrequested liver lecture and prescribing the plan ("decreasing the number of drinks... could be the best thing that you can do for your health") without asking the client's ideas or permission, and the client's "Well, I guess I'll try" is accepted without exploring his own goals.

nonjudgment.why: There is no overt shaming or labeling, but the therapist warns twice without being asked ("Alcohol can have some dangerous effects on your body... which you need to keep in mind") and argues when the client pushes back ("so do you see the connection there?"), giving repeated disapproving warnings and correction rather than neutral information.

empathy.why: The therapist dismisses the client's stated time constraints as "that sounds like a lot of excuses to me" and never reflects her perspective about her busy schedule or the two-hour reality, showing little or no attention to her experience.

autonomy.why: The therapist assumes the expert role and prescribes the plan ("you need to go about three to four times a week and really fit in that hour workout"), argues when the client offers an alternative view ("if it's gonna take you two hours, then it's gonna take you two hours"), and closes by setting an expectation ("I'm hoping that you're gonna be able to tell me that you went to the gym").

nonjudgment.why: The therapist openly labels and shames the client ("you're just a lot of talk," "stop being lazy about it and just do it," "that sounds like a lot of excuses to me"), which are clear Confront behaviors.

empathy.why: The therapist never reflects the client's perspective (e.g., wanting to be 'a normal college student', the roommate being asleep, worry about the $150), responding instead with 'What were you thinking when you got into your car...' and recitations of the report, showing little or no attention to the client's experience.

autonomy.why: The therapist fully assumes the expert/authority role, prescribing behavior and outcomes ('You need to take responsibility for your actions', 'you'll need to show that you're able to follow our rules... otherwise, you'll be suspended') and argues past the client's view without any collaboration or choice.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist repeatedly warns, blames, and moralizes, including 'you could have caused an accident and killed somebody', 'disappointing your parents. You don't want that to happen, do you?', and 'Your behavior is not what Minnesota State University expects', which are classic MITI Confront examples (guilt appeals, warnings, criticism).

empathy.why: Beyond generic lines like "you know, I get it. Like, we've all been there," the therapist dismisses Chris's stated worries ("Chris, come on. You're getting peer pressure?"; "You're a star player, who's going to pick on you?") and never reflects his fear of being ostracized or his own idea that "I should like go with different friend groups."

autonomy.why: The therapist sets the agenda and the solution from the start ("you have to stick by the rules," "maybe you can start leading as a non-drinker"), argues when Chris raises concerns, makes staying on the team conditional ("we got to have a deal here if you're going to be on the team"), and extracts a promise ("You promise?... Shake") instead of drawing out Chris's own plan.

nonjudgment.why: There is no outright shaming, but the therapist repeatedly confronts and dismisses Chris ("Chris, come on. You're getting peer pressure?") and leans on rule-enforcement warnings ("I can't be hearing reports about you drinking... I have to enforce them"), so the conversation has a disapproving, uneven-power tone.

empathy.why: The therapist cuts off the client's explanation ("Science fair project or not...") and never explores the rain, the project, or what the client was weighing, giving little or no attention to the client's perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the full expert role, lays down rules and a threat ("I don't tolerate it... if you do it again, I'm gonna tell your parents"), and argues when the client pushes back ("It's a big deal"), which is the classic righting reflex.

nonjudgment.why: The therapist shames and lectures ("What were you thinking?", "I thought you were smart, you're taking AP classes"), adds unrequested warnings about drinking, and issues a punitive threat, all of which are textbook MITI Confront.

empathy.why: The therapist brushes off the client's job-specific fear ('it's not really something you need to worry about'), and the token 'I-I-I understand that' is immediately followed by 'but like I said, it's very rare', so there is no reflection of what losing strength would mean for a truck driver who hauls heavy boxes.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and lays out the plan ('You- you really need to take it', 'make sure you go ahead and pick up your medicine... one every day'), and argues when the client offers an alternative ('I'll take it home and I'll think about it'), a clear righting reflex that ends in disengaged 'Whatever.'

nonjudgment.why: There is no shaming or labeling, but the therapist repeatedly disagrees with and corrects the client's concern and warns him ('the risk of stroke or heart attack is much worse', 'a stroke or heart attack is much worse'), the kind of uneven, argumentative pressure MITI codes as Confront.

empathy.why: The therapist never explores why Emily wanted the piercing ("Emily, why? Why did you get your lip pierced?" is a challenge, not curiosity), interrupts her repeatedly, and ignores her stated reasons ("I wanted a change", "it seems kind of cool"), giving little or no attention to her perspective.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role and prescribes the outcome ("You do not need a piercing", "it might not be a bad idea to reconsider the piercing"), argues when Emily pushes back ("Well, it's only been a month"), and ends with "you know where I stand on this," never acknowledging her choice even when she says "I wanted one."

nonjudgment.why: Some of the dental risk information is relevant, but it is delivered as disapproval, with repeated unrequested warnings ("it's something that we definitely don't like to see", "I'd hate to see you wreck your teeth for something like this"), a personal guilt appeal ("I've been seeing you for so long... I've watched you... mature"), and the closing reproach "you know where I stand on this." The guilt appeal and repeated disapproving warnings put this at the level of open moralizing.

empathy.why: The therapist makes only sporadic efforts to understand Scott: asking "You want to look different, or--?" briefly invites his view, but when he explains he'd "feel better" and fit his clothes, the therapist overrides it with "your health really, to me, it's more important than your looks," and never reflects his stated difficulty with being busy or out of the habit.

autonomy.why: The therapist takes the expert role throughout and lays out the plan: prescribing a pros/ideas list ("I think you just need to maybe sit down and write down a list"), offering their own routine as the model ("getting up an hour earlier... That's what I do"), and assigning homework ("that's what I'd like you to do"), without asking for Scott's ideas.

nonjudgment.why: There is no overt shaming, but the therapist repeatedly corrects and disagrees ("Well, I don't know about that"), tells Scott which of his reasons matter ("getting healthier is more important than sleep"), and frames the problem as willpower ("You just gotta do it"), all with clearly uneven power.
